what: The bounds the new-ship form types within, and the clamps the service applies, held to each other.
why: These are shape bounds rather than rules numbers - they bound what can be typed rather than
stating what a ship is - and docs/roadmap.md places them outside the content-policy render
guard deliberately, with that reason written down. What was missing is the other half of the
argument: each of them is written twice, once as a min/max on an input in ShipCard.tsx and once
as a Math.Clamp in the service, in two languages, with nothing holding the pair together.
A form whose max drifts above the service's clamp lets a player type a number that is silently
discarded on the way in. A form whose max drifts below it refuses a value the engine would have
accepted - which is the shape that made a stationary ship unturnable.
So the numbers live here once. shipFormBounds.test.tsx reads them off the rendered inputs and
ShipFormBoundsParityTests drives the service through CreateShip and reads the snapshot back.
Fire control's 6 is the one worth a sentence, because it is tighter than every neighbour and
sits in the range a rules number would. It is not one: no RulesProfile field carries it, the
profile editor has no cell for it, and fire control in this game is limited by what a hull can
carry rather than by a flat ceiling. It is recorded here as a shape bound so that the next
reader does not have to re-derive that, and so that if it is ever found to be a rulebook number
in disguise - as the screen ceiling of 3 was - there is one place to change.

bounds.label: Hull boxes
bounds.why: a ship of no boxes is not a ship, so this one floors at 1 rather than at unentered

bounds.label: Firecons
bounds.why: shape bound, not a rules ceiling: no profile field carries it and the game limits fire control by hull rather than by a flat number

bounds.label: Points (NPV)
bounds.why: shape bound on a number off the player's own design sheet
